rows: DSEAR requires risks of fire and explosion from dangerous substances connected with work to be eliminated or reduced.
DSEAR applies to workplaces that manufacture, store, process or use dangerous substances.
Employers must assess risks arising from dangerous substances.
Control measures should prevent releases and avoid ignition sources where reasonably practicable.
Mitigation should reduce the harmful effects of a fire, explosion or similar event.
Emergency arrangements should address foreseeable incidents involving dangerous substances.
Employees need suitable information, instruction and training about relevant hazards and controls.
DSEAR also covers gases under pressure and substances corrosive to metals within its amended scope.
General premises or land-use information does not prove that a dangerous substance or explosive atmosphere is present.
Applicability and control adequacy depend on substance classification, quantity, process, ventilation and ignition conditions.
PUWER requires work equipment to be suitable for its intended use.
Work equipment must be maintained in a safe condition.
Inspection is required where installation or deterioration could create safety risks.
Equipment should be used only by people with adequate information, instruction and training.
Protective devices, controls, isolation, markings and warnings must be provided where necessary.
Access to dangerous machinery parts should be prevented or movement stopped before a person enters the danger zone.
Safeguarding can include fixed or interlocked guards, two-hand controls, light guards and pressure-sensitive mats.
Users must manage residual risks identified by the machinery supplier.
PUWER covers equipment use and control; it does not establish that every machine at a premises is compliant.
Actual compliance depends on the machine, task, safeguards, maintenance, inspection and user competence.
RPE protects against airborne contaminants such as dust, mist, gas, vapour or fume.
Breathing apparatus may be needed where oxygen levels are inadequate.
RPE must be adequate for the hazard and reduce exposure to the required level.
RPE must be suitable for the wearer, task and environment.
Selection requires knowledge of contaminant type, concentration and physical form.
Other PPE, spectacles, facial characteristics and work demands can affect suitability.
Tight-fitting facepieces require appropriate fit testing.
RPE must be maintained, stored and used in accordance with instruction and training.
RPE should not be treated as proof that exposure has been controlled without task and exposure evidence.
An address cannot establish face fit, filter class, wear time, oxygen level or contaminant concentration.
Construction dust can cause serious and irreversible lung disease.
COSHH requires employers to assess, control and review risks from hazardous construction dust.
Common high-risk dusts include silica dust, wood dust and lower-toxicity general dust.
Controls should prioritise eliminating or reducing dust generation.
Water suppression and on-tool extraction can reduce airborne dust.
Extraction equipment must have suitable performance and secure, leak-free connections.
Some high-dust tasks also require suitable RPE.
Tight-fitting masks used for construction dust require fit testing.
Construction activity or building type alone does not establish worker exposure or control effectiveness.
Risk depends on material, task, duration, tool, ventilation, extraction, RPE and supervision.
